sections.overview: This small African forest pangolin climbs trees but also descends to forage; current specialist sources use Phataginus tricuspis, though older references used Manis.
sections.identification: Its body is protected by overlapping scales and its belly has pale, sparsely haired skin; compared with the black-bellied pangolin (Phataginus tetradactyla), its tail is shorter.
sections.habitat: It occurs in equatorial African forests and uses trees as well as the ground.
sections.diet: It feeds mainly on ants and termites, which it collects with its long sticky tongue.
sections.behavior: It climbs and can use its prehensile tail for support; when threatened, it curls into a ball and shields its soft underside with scales.
sections.reproduction: A single young is usually born after a gestation of about 150 days and rides on its mother’s tail.
sections.ecology: By eating ants and termites, it participates in forest food webs, but population monitoring remains difficult.
sections.conservation: The IUCN SSC lists it as Endangered; hunting and trade threaten it, though local trends remain unclear.
